Below is a draft essay. Revise it so that it reads as if a US grade 8 student wrote it in class for a timed writing test. Keep the position it argues and keep it at about 462 words. The file must contain only the revised essay.

Draft:

Dear Principal,

I am writing to urge you to adopt the first policy under consideration: allowing students to bring phones to school and use them during lunch and other free times, provided the phones stay off during class. A full ban may seem like the safer choice, but it asks too much of students and does too little for the school.

The strongest reason for Policy 1 is that it treats students as responsible young people. Most of us already carry phones everywhere, and we are expected to manage them outside school. A total ban removes the chance to practice that judgment in a setting where teachers are close by to help if something goes wrong. Students who learn to put a phone away during class and pick it back up at lunch are building a habit they will need in college and at work.

Policy 1 also serves real needs. Parents want to reach their children after a bus is late, a ride falls through, or a family emergency comes up. Under a total ban, a student who needs to make one quick call must go through the front office, which pulls staff away from their work and can make an ordinary problem feel urgent. Under Policy 1, a student can simply send a message. Phones also help with schoolwork outside class. Students can check a homework assignment, look up a word they do not know, or photograph a board they could not copy in time.

Some worry that phones will distract students during lunch, or that they will lead to bullying and cheating. These concerns are real, but a ban does not solve them. Students who want to misuse a phone can do so at home, on the bus, or in the bathroom, where no one can see them. The better approach is to set clear rules: phones must stay in bags during class, any photograph or recording of another student without permission brings consequences, and devices confiscated for violations are returned only to a parent. These rules target the behavior that causes harm rather than punishing every student for the actions of a few.

Finally, a total ban is hard to enforce. Teachers would spend class time checking pockets and backpacks, and students would learn to hide their phones rather than follow the rule. A policy that most students follow is worth more than a stricter one that nobody respects.

For these reasons, I ask you to choose Policy 1. Let students use their phones in the free time they already have, hold them to clear expectations during class, and trust them to meet those expectations. I would be glad to help draft the guidelines or share student views on how the rules should work.

Respectfully,

A Concerned Student
